blocks.prompt: Every Raindrop Has Been Up and Down Before
blocks.text: The sun shines on the sea and on lakes. It warms the water at the top. Tiny bits of that water float up into the sky, so small that you cannot see them go. High up, the air is cold. The floating water cools down and turns back into little drops. Millions of drops together make a cloud. Inside the cloud, the drops bump into each other and stick. They grow. When a drop gets too heavy for the air to hold, it falls. That is rain. It lands in the sea and in lakes, and then the sun starts it all over again.

blocks.prompt: The Drop That Is Not a Teardrop
blocks.text: Draw a raindrop and you will probably draw a teardrop: round at the bottom, pointed at the top. Almost every picture of rain looks like that. It is wrong. Photographs taken with very fast cameras show something else. A small raindrop is a ball, round like a tiny marble. As a drop grows bigger, the air pushing up against it flattens the bottom. Now it looks like the top half of a hamburger bun, or a kidney bean. If a drop grows wider than a pea, the air pushing on it tears it into smaller drops. So why do we draw the pointed shape? Because water hanging from a faucet makes that shape as it lets go. We drew the drop leaving, then we drew rain the same way, and nobody checked for a very long time. Rain falls fast. A big drop can hit the ground at twenty miles an hour, about as quick as you can ride a bike down a hill.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: About a million cloud droplets make one raindrop
Every drop forms around a speck of dust or salt
Those specks are called condensation nuclei
Droplets merge as they fall: coalescence
Virga is rain that dries up before it lands

blocks.prompt: How to Build a Raindrop
blocks.text: A cloud is not made of rain. A cloud is made of droplets so small that about a million of them would fit inside a single raindrop. Those droplets are light enough that the slow, rising air inside a cloud simply holds them up. A cloud can float above you for hours without dropping anything at all. For rain to happen, a droplet has to grow, and to grow it first needs something to grow on. Water vapor will not turn into liquid in clean air easily. It needs a speck: a grain of desert dust, a crystal of sea salt flung up by a breaking wave, a bit of pollen, a particle of smoke. Scientists call these specks condensation nuclei. Almost every raindrop that has ever landed on your head was built around one. Once a droplet forms, it drifts. It collides with other droplets and merges with them, a process called coalescence. Bigger droplets fall faster than smaller ones, so they catch up to the little ones and sweep them up on the way down. The drop grows heavier. Eventually the rising air cannot hold it any longer, and it falls out of the bottom of the cloud. Even then, the trip is not guaranteed. In dry desert air, a drop can evaporate on the way down and vanish before it ever reaches the ground. Forecasters call that virga, and you can spot it from far away: gray streaks hanging under a cloud, ending in midair.

notes: Petrichor: the name for the smell of rain
Coined in 1964 by Bear and Thomas in Nature
From Greek petra, stone, and ichor, the gods' blood
Geosmin is made by bacteria in the soil
Our noses detect geosmin at 5 parts per trillion
The smell before a storm is ozone, not rain

blocks.prompt: The Smell of Rain Has a Name
blocks.text: You can smell rain before you see it. Almost everyone can. The strange part is that water has no smell at all, so whatever you are smelling is not the rain. In 1964, two Australian scientists, Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Thomas, published a paper in the journal Nature about that smell. They gave it a name: petrichor. They built the word out of Greek. Petra means stone. Ichor was the fluid said to run in the veins of the gods. The smell of rain on dry stone, more or less. Most of the smell comes from two sources. The first is oil. During long dry spells, plants shed oily compounds that soak into clay and rock. When rain finally arrives, the water pushes those trapped oils back out into the air. The second source is a chemical called geosmin, and geosmin is not made by plants at all. It is made by bacteria living in the soil. When the ground dries out, those bacteria make spores, and geosmin comes with them. Human noses are extraordinarily tuned to geosmin. We can detect it at about five parts per trillion, which is roughly a teaspoon dropped into four hundred Olympic swimming pools. Nobody is certain why we are that sensitive. Some scientists suspect our distant ancestors used the scent to find water, and that the sensitivity stuck around long after we stopped needing it. There is a mechanical part to the story too. In 2015, researchers at MIT filmed raindrops landing on soil using high-speed cameras. Each drop traps a cushion of air underneath it as it hits. That air escapes as tiny bubbles which burst upward, throwing a fine mist of scent-carrying droplets into the breeze. Rain does not just release the smell. It launches it. The sharp, clean smell that arrives just before a storm is something different again. That one is ozone, carried down from high in the sky by the storm's own falling air.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: The Arthashastra taxed farmers by measured rainfall
Korea's cheugugi standardized rain gauges in 1441
A standard gauge stretches 1 inch of rain into 10
Mawsynram, India averages about 467 inches a year
Meghalaya means abode of clouds
Monsoon comes from the Arabic word mawsim, season

blocks.prompt: The Bowl Outside the Storehouse
blocks.text: Rain is the only weather that people have measured carefully, deliberately, and on purpose for thousands of years. Not because it is beautiful. Because everything depends on it. The oldest known instructions come from an ancient Indian book on how to run a state, the Arthashastra, written more than two thousand years ago. It tells officials to keep a bowl of a fixed size outside the storehouse and to record what collects in it, because the tax a farmer owed ought to depend on the rain that farmer actually received. A dry year and a wet year are not the same year, and a government that cannot tell them apart will take grain from people who have none. The idea was rebuilt, far more precisely, in Korea. In 1441, the court of King Sejong ordered a standard rain gauge called the cheugugi: a cylinder of fixed width and depth, set on a stone pedestal at a fixed height, and distributed to offices across the kingdom. That last detail is the important one. One person with a bucket learns about their own yard. Hundreds of people with identical buckets, at identical heights, all reporting to one place, learn about a country. Korea holds some of the longest rainfall records in the world because of that decision. Modern gauges still use a trick worth understanding. The standard gauge is a funnel eight inches across draining into a tube with one tenth the area. An inch of rain in the funnel stands ten inches deep in the tube. The rain has not changed. The instrument has stretched it, so that a person reading the side of the tube can see hundredths of an inch that would otherwise be invisible. Good measurement is often just a clever shape. What the measurements reveal is that rain is handed out with almost unreasonable unfairness. Mawsynram, in the Indian state of Meghalaya, averages around 467 inches of rain a year. The name Meghalaya means abode of clouds. Meanwhile parts of Chile's Atacama Desert average less than a tenth of an inch a year, and some weather stations there have gone years without recording any rain at all. The ground is so dry that engineers test Mars equipment in it. Both places sit on the same planet, under the same sun, doing exactly what the wind and the mountains tell them to do. For much of humanity the stakes are not academic. The word monsoon comes from the Arabic mawsim, meaning season. India's summer monsoon delivers roughly three quarters of the country's yearly rain in about four months. A monsoon that arrives two weeks late, or drops a fifth less water than usual, is not a weather story. It is a food story, an electricity story, and an economy story, for well over a billion people. Which is why the bowl outside the storehouse still matters. Every satellite and radar dish we have ever built is checked against a number that someone, somewhere, read off the side of a tube.
